accepted.title: Select cardiac assessment after an abnormal screen

record.title: Select cardiac assessment after an abnormal screen
fairness: Monitored reassessment without immediate imaging is the best of these plans: the conduction finding is unchanged from before injury, and the current course does not supply an additional structural or ischemic imaging indication. The elevated troponin is not dismissed.

The task now compares additional imaging while telemetry and serial biomarkers are shared care; it no longer falsely treats those measures as mutually exclusive with echocardiography. TTE could become appropriate with a changed clinical question, but that does not make routine immediate TTE the best answer here.

Two consequential judgments remain: distinguish an old ECG abnormality from the new biomarker finding, then apply current physiology to the imaging decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The subsequent arrhythmia and nondiagnostic TTE introduce new information. This explanation does not name TEE or give away the later modality choice.

accepted.title: Escalate thoracic bleeding care from physiology

record.title: Escalate thoracic bleeding care from physiology
fairness: Thoracotomy is the best of the offered hemorrhage-control approaches in the repeated loss-of-perfusion course. Low drain output is not reliable reassurance when a large collection remains and blood pressure depends on continuing transfusion.

The two consequential steps are to reject a misleading drainage-output interpretation, then use physiological instability to choose the operative approach over thoracoscopy or an embolization pathway.
The alternatives are parallel procedures addressing hemostasis. Necessary perfusion and alternative-source observations are not wording-only cues; they discriminate clinically meaningful paths.
The next node explicitly establishes successful hemostasis and a later stable state. This explanation does not disclose the later retained-clot treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Preserve the mismatch between low drainage and ongoing physiological failure. Do not replace it with an unsupported exact output threshold.
Optional tightening: the current-update sentence can be shortened while retaining that drainage and blood replacement have occurred.

accepted.title: Reassess rib stabilization after failed liberation

record.title: Reassess rib stabilization after failed liberation
fairness: Rib stabilization is a defensible best next addition among the offered plans after recovery from shock, persistent severely displaced segmental fractures, improving pulmonary findings and failed liberation despite analgesic care.

The learner must distinguish improving parenchymal injury from persistent chest-wall mechanical failure, then choose correction of that barrier rather than simply repeat support or commit to prolonged weaning. Both the interval improvement and actual failed trials matter.

Paradoxical movement is a legitimate necessary observation, not a diagnosis label. The known fracture pattern does not by itself answer the question; current physiological recovery and failure despite treatment determine why reassessment is appropriate now.

The active update supplies the preceding recovery, fracture morphology, treatment and failed trials; it stands alone without the parked shock-priority node. No preceding fixation feedback supplies the answer.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The key should be interpreted as the next treatment strategy, not a guarantee that stabilization produces successful extubation; the explanation appropriately uses 'supports ... assessment'.
suggestions: Preserve the contrast between improving lung findings and persistent mechanical failure during actual trials.
Keep clinician confirmation of operative candidacy and avoid unsupported exact timing thresholds. Do not promise ventilator liberation as an inevitable outcome of stabilization.

record.title: AAA screening after incompletely covering CTA
fairness: The best offered answer is abdominal aortic ultrasound. The resident must recognize that acquisition ending at the celiac origin does not assess the infrarenal aorta, then apply preventive screening to an asymptomatic 69-year-old male former smoker. The examination title does not establish adequate prior screening.

CTA is a credible modality error and no additional imaging is a credible coverage error. Both imaging labels contain abdominal aortic, so lexical overlap does not uniquely identify ultrasound. The acquisition endpoint is necessary evidence, not an authored interpretation.

The retrospective visit and requested plan are clear; this standalone node does not need a prior answer. Screening eligibility and examination coverage are high-yield concepts, although the reasoning is moderate rather than hard.

accepted.title: Persistent hypertension after rate response in acute dissection

record.title: Persistent hypertension after rate response in acute dissection
fairness: Adding intravenous nicardipine is the best offered change. The resident must distinguish an achieved rate response from persistent severe hypertension, then select additional pressure reduction while retaining initial beta blockade.

Increasing esmolol is a credible attempt to treat the residual pressure with the existing infusion. Diltiazem is a neighboring rate-control alternative. The unchanged PR interval, warm extremities and preserved systolic function do not supply a reason to replace the beta blocker.
The three choices are specific infusion actions of comparable length. Nicardipine is not named in the pre-answer record and there is no nonmedical wording shortcut to its pharmacology.

The known dissection anatomy appropriately frames a different treatment-response task. This standalone revision has no preceding explanation that supplies its answer. Sequencing rate and pressure control is high yield; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

accepted.title: Preserving pedicled LIMA inflow during elective TEVAR

record.title: Preserving pedicled LIMA inflow during elective TEVAR
fairness: The learner must infer coronary dependence on subclavian inflow and then distinguish two prophylactic revascularization techniques, rather than merely recognize the risk of arm ischemia.

A patent pedicled LIMA and occluded native LAD provide a defensible reason to prefer bypass over transposition involving proximal subclavian interruption. The delayed-bypass option is less appropriate because arm symptoms do not monitor the threatened coronary territory. The two before-coverage options prevent timing alone from identifying the key.
suggestions: Retain the pedicled graft origin, patency and native LAD status. Keep the explanation specific to this coronary-dependent anatomy rather than declaring transposition universally unsuitable.
